galvanize

GAL-vuh-nyze · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To galvanize is to shock or excite into sudden action.

News of the endangered species finally being spotted again seemed to galvanize the whole town into supporting the new nature preserve.

Example

A single photograph of the flooded elementary school was enough to galvanize thousands of strangers online into donating supplies within twenty-four hours.

The photo didn't just inform people -- it jolted them into immediate, energetic action. That sudden shock into activity is exactly what galvanize captures.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

energize: To energize people is to fill them with fresh energy and vitality, the way rest or good news can. Galvanize is more sudden and more pointed: a shock that jolts a group into acting right now, not just feeling livelier.

stir: To stir is to awaken a feeling gently — a speech stirs hope, an old song stirs memories. It is the faint beginning of movement, while galvanize is a jolt that has a whole crowd up and acting at once.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

lull: to calm or soothe into a relaxed, inactive state

discourage: to drain someone's confidence or motivation

Where it sits · how strong the jolt into action — encourage → galvanize → electrify

encourage vs. galvanize: To encourage someone is a gentle nudge of support — far softer than galvanize, which jolts people into sudden action.

electrify vs. galvanize: To electrify a crowd is an even more intense, almost overwhelming version of the same excited-energy image galvanize suggests.

Build the Word

The pieces

proper noun root — Galvani

proper noun root — Galvani: Luigi Galvani, the 18th-century Italian scientist who discovered that electric current could make a dead frog's muscles twitch (Italian (eponym))

suffix — -ze (-ize)

suffix — -ze (-ize): to make, to cause to be (Greek)

Put it together

Put it together: Galvanize is named after Luigi Galvani, who discovered that an electric shock could make a dead frog's leg twitch, plus the -ize verb ending (spelled -ze here, sharing its i with Galvani). The word first meant 'to stimulate with electricity' and later came to mean shocking a person or group into sudden action.

Use the root in a new word: galvanic

Use the root in a new word: galvanic: The speech had a galvanic effect on the room, and within minutes every hand was raised to volunteer.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Galvanize almost always carries a positive, energizing charge -- it describes rousing people to act for a cause, not frightening or provoking them into conflict. Compare it with goad, which also pushes someone toward action but through negative needling rather than inspiring energy.
